messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down, Conflict: Confrontations, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Thien's Vigilance

Thien was seventy-six years old and had lived in the United States for forty-two years, but the war had never truly left Cambodia. He arrived at the intake appointment on a Tuesday morning in November, moving slowly through the clinic waiting room with the careful deliberation of a man who had learned long ago to notice every exit, every person, every sound. His hands trembled slightly as he filled out the intake form, and the receptionist noticed he gripped the pen as though it might escape.

The traumatic event itself was seared into his memory with a clarity that had only sharpened with age. In April 1975, when Thien was thirty-four years old, Khmer Rouge soldiers had come to his neighborhood in Phnom Penh in the early morning. He had been asleep when they burst through his door—four men in black, faces obscured, moving with the mechanical efficiency of people who had done this many times before. They had separated him from his wife and two children without explanation, bound his wrists with cord so tight that his hands had swollen within minutes, and forced him into a truck with thirty other men. The cord had cut off circulation; he could still feel the phantom sensation of his fingers going numb, the panic of not knowing if they would ever work again. They had driven for hours. Men around him were crying, praying, begging. The smell—sweat, fear, human waste from those who had lost control of their bodies—had filled the truck bed with an acrid, suffocating density that he could conjure in an instant even now, decades later.

He had survived, though he never learned why. He had spent three years in labor camps, had seen executions, had watched men die of starvation and disease. But it was that first day—the sudden violence, the restraint, the helplessness—that his nervous system had never forgotten.

For the past several years, Thien had worked the night shift at a warehouse in Newark, managing inventory for a pharmaceutical distributor. The work was solitary and suited him; he preferred the quiet hours after midnight when the building was nearly empty. But six months ago, a new supervisor named Marcus had been hired, a man in his forties with a loud voice and an aggressive management style. Marcus believed in "accountability," which meant confrontations on the warehouse floor—raising his voice, getting in workers' faces, sometimes physically blocking them from leaving a conversation. Thien had begun to dread his shifts. When Marcus approached him with anger in his expression, something in Thien's chest would seize. His breathing would become shallow. He had started calling in sick, inventing reasons to avoid the days when Marcus was scheduled. His supervisor had noticed; there had been a formal conversation about reliability. Thien was now at risk of losing a job he had held for eight years.

The triggers came without warning and with devastating force. Last month, a coworker had accidentally brushed against him in the storage aisle, steadying himself with a hand on Thien's shoulder. Thien had gone rigid, his heart racing, and had excused himself to the bathroom where he sat in a stall for twenty minutes unable to move. Two weeks before that, he had been standing in line at the supermarket when a man behind him had stepped too close, and the proximity alone—the sense of being trapped between the man and the register—had sent him back to the truck bed, to the smell of fear and waste, to the cord cutting into his wrists. He had abandoned his groceries and left.

The memories themselves were the worst part. They did not come gently or in fragments. When they came, they came complete and overwhelming—the faces of the soldiers, the weight of the cord, the smell so vivid he could taste it. His body would flood with adrenaline. His hands would shake uncontrollably. He had learned that once a memory had seized him, he could not simply push through it; he had to stop whatever he was doing and wait for it to release him, which sometimes took hours. He had missed appointments, had sat paralyzed at his kitchen table, had called in to work claiming illness when really he was trapped inside his own nervous system.

What had finally brought him to the clinic was a moment of clarity born from desperation. He had realized, with the cold certainty of age, that he did not have unlimited time left, and he was spending what remained of it imprisoned by events from nearly fifty years ago. He was afraid—terrified, really—that he would die this way, reactive and isolated, his life constricted to the hours when he felt safe enough to exist. But there was something else too, something that surfaced when he allowed himself to hope: the possibility that the cord around his wrists might finally, after all these decades, loosen its grip.
